From Shared Patterns to Individual Evidence: Two-Stage Reasoning for Emerging Entities in Temporal Knowledge Graphs

Jinchuan Zhang1, Lei Gao1, Hongyu Jiang1, Chong Mu1, Chenang Cai1, Ke Yan1† Affiliation: 1School of Computer Science and Engineering,
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China
Email: {jc.zhang, muchong, kyan}@uestc.edu.cn,
{leigao, hyjiang}@std.uestc.edu.cn,
{caichenang}@hotmail.com
†Corresponding author: Ke Yan.
Abstract.

Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint role asymmetry that degrades unseen answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query-side and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight evidence adapter (EA) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support-stratified and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query micro and answer entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%16.73\%–88.83%88.83\% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%8.28\%–32.63%32.63\%, Answer-new MRR by 7.81%7.81\%–41.24%41.24\%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%9.64\%–39.94%39.94\%, gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE.

1. Introduction

Real-world relational event streams, ranging from geopolitical repositories such as ICEWS and GDELT to evolving distributed graph systems, are modeled as temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) of timestamped quadruples (h,r,o,t)(h,r,o,t) (Ma et al., 2026; Song et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2021; Tian et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2025). Temporal extrapolation forecasts future links (h,r,?,t)(h,r,?,t) from strictly past facts prior to tt by ranking candidate entities across a catalog (Jin et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025a). While recent models capture snapshot evolution, multigraph dependencies, logical rules, and histories relevant to the query (Jin et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), continuous streams constantly introduce new actors whose histories are initially absent and accumulate sparsely (Wang et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023b; Lin et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a). Consequently, forecasting in dynamic streams hinges on the few-shot temporal reasoning problem: predicting reliably over entities that transition from zero-shot debuts to sparse, unevenly observed trajectories.

Empirical profiling across four standard benchmarks exposes a sharp structural tension, as illustrated in Figure 1(c) (with complete statistics in the supplemental material). At the identity level, entities first observed during the test interval constitute 13.33%13.33\%–25.20%25.20\% of test-active actors; however, at the traffic level, queries touching a zero-support endpoint represent only 0.166%0.166\%–4.54%4.54\% of evaluated queries. Furthermore, emergence extends well beyond an entity’s first appearance: on ICEWS05–15, 83.32%83.32\% of test queries targeting test-emergent answer entities occur after debut under limited positive support, whereas on ICEWS18 70.35%70.35\% remain at zero support. Hence, emerging-entity reasoning spans a continuous spectrum from zero-shot priors to sparse few-shot evidence.

To illustrate this dilemma concretely, Figure 1(a)–(b) tracks the emerging entity Takata in ICEWS14, which is preregistered in the candidate catalog with textual metadata prior to its first recorded interaction (Zhao et al., 2026). At its debut (t=310t=310), Takata has zero graph history (no=0n_{o}=0). Whereas querying an unseen head can transfer interaction patterns from semantically related actors, ranking Takata as the ground-truth answer to (Newspaper (Japan), Make statement, ?, 310310) requires it to outrank thousands of richly observed catalog competitors. Subsequently, before the follow-up query (Japan, Make statement, ?, 332332), Takata accumulates only six sparse facts spanning t=310t=310–330330: two early isolated interactions (t=310,317t=310,317), an independent statement from Jay Rockefeller (t=328t=328), and repeated contacts from the U.S. government including two identical Demand events (t=323,330t=323,330). Because short sliding windows discard those earlier sparse facts while independent aggregation overcounts the repeated demands, both heuristics skew Takata’s latent state.

However, existing temporal inductive methods address only isolated ends of this continuum. Pattern transfer models such as TransFIR (Zhao et al., 2026) map unseen entities to semantic interaction clusters at debut, yet omit event-updated candidate memory across the catalog. In contrast, online memory models such as AdaTKG (Lee et al., 2026) update per-entity exponential moving average (EMA) states, yet exhibit pronounced endpoint role asymmetry: across all four benchmarks (Table 3), AdaTKG improves unseen query prediction (Query-new) over TransFIR while consistently degrading unseen answer ranking (Answer-new), dropping by 57.6%57.6\% on GDELT (0.0801→0.03400.0801\to 0.0340). Therefore, bridging shared patterns with individual evidence requires resolving three coupled challenges:

C1: Heterogeneous history availability and role asymmetry. Within any timestamp batch, query heads and catalog candidates span zero-support newcomers and mature actors. Restricting memory readout to active query heads leaves competing candidates misaligned, whereas naive memory fusion causes excessive reliance on history when observations are absent.

C2: Long-range sparsity versus bursty evidence redundancy. Early interactions are simultaneously sparse across long temporal spans and correlated within short bursts. Updating a high-capacity pattern encoder with sparse gradients risks overfitting; conversely, independent aggregation lets repetitive bursts overwhelm informative facts.

C3: Long-tail supervision dilution and micro-averaged evaluation. Since low-support queries occupy a small fraction of natural batches, standard cross-entropy is dominated by high-support entities and neglects asymmetric endpoint roles (Query-new, Answer-new, Both-new). In addition, conventional micro averaging over queries masks systematic errors on infrequent emerging identities.

To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage framework decoupling low-variance shared-pattern learning from lightweight posterior refinement for individual entities. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the entire candidate catalog, inclusive of non-query candidates, while applying coupled query-side and catalog-side availability masking during training (C1). Subsequently, in Stage II, we freeze the Stage I predictor to prevent sparse overfitting and train a lightweight Evidence Adaptation (EA) module. Specifically, EA combines a textual semantic prior with bounded long-range evidence over the full revealed prefix, discounts bursty redundancy via a descriptor Gram matrix covariance model, and adds a strictly positively scaled translational Gaussian compatibility residual to full-catalog scores (C2). Stage II is trained offline under support-stratified and role-balanced co-answer supervision equipped with training-only prior-odds debiasing across support buckets and soft residual alignment to prevent prior shortcuts induced by balanced losses, whereas evaluation drops the training bias, keeps parameters frozen, and updates persistent states strictly after each timestamp is scored (C3).

Across ICEWS14, ICEWS18, ICEWS05–15, and GDELT, INSPIRE attains Emerging MRRs of 0.22640.2264, 0.18770.1877, 0.25870.2587, and 0.16230.1623, improving over the strongest baseline by 34.48%34.48\%, 32.15%32.15\%, 16.73%16.73\%, and 88.83%88.83\%. Relative to paired Stage I predictors (INSPIRE w/o EA), EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%8.28\%–32.63%32.63\%, Query-new MRR by 9.29%9.29\%–21.94%21.94\%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%9.64\%–39.94%39.94\%, while also improving overall test MRR on every dataset. Notably, EA achieves substantial calibrated gains (+7.81%+7.81\%–+41.24%+41.24\%) on Answer-new queries where the true answer has zero prior events. Nevertheless, our functional decomposition resolves this apparent paradox, showing that these gains are attributed jointly to the learned semantic prior and candidate score competition, whereby correlated posterior updates demote mismatched established competitors without inflating a blanket zero-support bias.

Our contributions are threefold:

  1. (1)

    Availability-aware shared-pattern learning. We formulate emerging-entity reasoning across the continuum from zero-shot to few-shot reasoning and introduce catalog-wide gated memory fusion with coordinated query-side and catalog-side masking to resolve role asymmetry.

  2. (2)

    Correlated Bayesian evidence adaptation. We build a lightweight residual adapter over a frozen predictor combining textual priors, bounded long-range queues, and Gram matrix correlation weighting with balanced supervision.

  3. (3)

    Longitudinal evaluation and mechanism dissection. We evaluate endpoint roles and emerging-answer cohorts via micro and entity macro metrics on four event benchmarks, isolating how candidate competition drives zero-support gains.

2. Problem Formulation

2.1. Temporal Extrapolation for Emerging Entities

A TKG is an event stream ℱ⊆ℰ×ℛ×ℰ×𝒯\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{T}, where ℰ\mathcal{E}, ℛ\mathcal{R}, and 𝒯\mathcal{T} denote the entity catalog, relation set, and ordered timestamp set. Each quadruple (h,r,o,t)∈ℱ(h,r,o,t)\in\mathcal{F} records an interaction from head hh to tail oo under relation rr at timestamp tt. Let ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} collect facts at timestamp tt and ℋ<t=⋃τ<tℱτ\mathcal{H}_{<t}=\bigcup_{\tau<t}\mathcal{F}_{\tau} denote the strictly past revealed prefix. Given query q=(h,r,?,t)q=(h,r,?,t) and ℋ<t\mathcal{H}_{<t}, temporal extrapolation ranks all catalog candidates o∈ℰo\in\mathcal{E} using past events and fixed textual vectors for entity names xe∈ℝdxx_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}.

Consistent problem boundary. Following the standard emerging-entity benchmark of TransFIR (Zhao et al., 2026) and AdaTKG (Lee et al., 2026), we retain original timestamps split chronologically into training (50%50\%), validation (20%20\%), and test (30%30\%) intervals, with candidate catalog ℰ\mathcal{E} and fixed textual vectors {xe}e∈ℰ\{x_{e}\}_{e\in\mathcal{E}} available prior to an entity’s first interaction (emergence). At each timestamp tt, every fact (h,r,o,t)∈ℱt(h,r,o,t)\in\mathcal{F}_{t} forms a forward tail query (h,r,?,t)(h,r,?,t) (answer oo) and an inverse head query (o,r−1,?,t)(o,r^{-1},?,t) (answer hh). Let ℬtd\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d} denote the directional query batch for d∈{fwd,inv}d\in\{\mathrm{fwd},\mathrm{inv}\} and 𝒰td={h:(h,r,t)∈ℬtd}\mathcal{U}_{t}^{d}=\{h:(h,r,t)\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d}\} its active query heads. Accordingly, both directions are scored over the full catalog ℰ\mathcal{E} using only (h,r,t)∈ℬtd(h,r,t)\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d}, 𝒰td\mathcal{U}_{t}^{d}, and ℋ<t\mathcal{H}_{<t} strictly before ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} is revealed; labels are used exclusively for training losses or ranking after scoring. During evaluation, learned parameters remain frozen while revealed events ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} subsequently advance persistent states for future timestamps, and raw full-catalog bidirectional ranks are computed under the released history construction pipeline (Zhao et al., 2026) across all comparators.

2.2. Evaluation Protocol

To trace entities from zero-shot debut through sparse few-shot evolution, we define the observed support of entity e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E} before timestamp tt as

(1) ne(t)=∑(h,r,o,τ)∈ℋ<t[e∈{h,o}],n_{e}(t)=\sum_{(h,r,o,\tau)\in\mathcal{H}_{<t}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[e\in\{h,o\}\right],

counting distinct original incident facts strictly before tt (self-loops count once, whereas inverse queries add no observations). Hence, ne​(t)n_{e}(t) reflects lifetime revealed support independently of finite model history windows.

Asymmetric endpoint roles. Queries touching at least one zero-support endpoint decompose into three disjoint roles: (1) Query-new (nh​(t)=0,no​(t)>0n_{h}(t)=0,\ n_{o}(t)>0): an unobserved query head predicts an established answer; (2) Answer-new (nh​(t)>0,no​(t)=0n_{h}(t)>0,\ n_{o}(t)=0): an established head ranks an unobserved answer over ℰ\mathcal{E}; and (3) Both-new (nh​(t)=0,no​(t)=0n_{h}(t)=0,\ n_{o}(t)=0): both endpoints have zero prior support. Their union defines the Emerging query set. Although bidirectional evaluation gives Query-new and Answer-new identical query counts, they nevertheless test asymmetric tasks: Query-new initiates prediction from an unseen source, whereas Answer-new requires an unobserved candidate to outrank thousands of established actors.

Longitudinal emerging-answer cohort and metrics. Let first⁡(e)\operatorname{first}(e) be the earliest timestamp at which ee appears in an original fact. For an evaluation interval SS with query set 𝒬S\mathcal{Q}_{S}, the emerging-answer cohort 𝒞S\mathcal{C}_{S} and its longitudinal query set 𝒬𝒞S\mathcal{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_{S}} are

(2) 𝒞S={e∈ℰ:first⁡(e)∈S},𝒬𝒞S={q∈𝒬S:a⁡(q)∈𝒞S},\mathcal{C}_{S}=\{e\in\mathcal{E}:\operatorname{first}(e)\in S\},\qquad\mathcal{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_{S}}=\{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{S}:a(q)\in\mathcal{C}_{S}\},

where a⁡(q)a(q) is the ground-truth answer of qq. Consequently, 𝒬𝒞S\mathcal{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_{S}} tracks every answer occurrence of test-emergent identities across debut (no​(t)=0n_{o}(t)=0) and post-emergence support strata (11, 22–55, 66–1010, >10>10).

For any query collection 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, let ℰ𝒬={a⁡(q):q∈𝒬}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}=\{a(q):q\in\mathcal{Q}\} and 𝒬e={q∈𝒬:a⁡(q)=e}\mathcal{Q}_{e}=\{q\in\mathcal{Q}:a(q)=e\}. To prevent frequent actors from dominating aggregate scores, we pair query micro MRR (MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}}) with answer entity macro MRR (MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}}) over raw full-catalog ranks rank⁡(q)\operatorname{rank}(q):

(3) MRRmicro⁡(𝒬)\displaystyle\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}}(\mathcal{Q}) =1|𝒬|​∑q∈𝒬1rank⁡(q),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\frac{1}{\operatorname{rank}(q)},
MRRmacro⁡(𝒬)\displaystyle\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}}(\mathcal{Q}) =1|ℰ𝒬|​∑e∈ℰ𝒬1|𝒬e|​∑q∈𝒬e1rank⁡(q).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}|}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}_{e}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{e}}\frac{1}{\operatorname{rank}(q)}.

While MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}} weights queries equally, MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} weights each distinct answer identity equally over its full trajectory in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, thereby exposing whether gains extend to infrequent emerging actors.

2.3. Empirical Diagnosis and Research Questions

Figure 1(c) reveals two defining properties of few-shot emergence across the four benchmarks. First, regarding identity–traffic skew, test-emergent entities account for 13.33%13.33\%–25.20%25.20\% of active identities, whereas Emerging queries occupy only 0.166%0.166\%–4.54%4.54\% of directed test records; hence, standard training losses severely underweight emerging identities. Second, regarding dual zero-shot and few-shot regimes, post-emergence workload varies markedly across horizons: on the 11-year ICEWS05–15 stream, 10,20610{,}206 of 12,24912{,}249 cohort queries (83.32%83.32\%) occur after the emerging answer acquires positive support, whereas on ICEWS18 zero-support debuts still comprise 70.35%70.35\% of cohort queries.

Core hypothesis and research questions. Therefore, we hypothesize that decoupling availability-aware shared patterns from correlation-weighted Bayesian adaptation resolves role asymmetry and bursty few-shot sparsity without overfitting high-capacity encoders. Accordingly, we investigate this hypothesis through six research questions:

  • •

    RQ1 (Effectiveness and Role Asymmetry): Does two-stage decoupling improve Emerging ranking and repair the Answer-new degradation of existing temporal inductive baselines?

  • •

    RQ2 (Availability-Aware Shared Patterns): How do gated memory fusion, full-catalog readout, and availability masking shape Stage I and support Stage II adaptation?

  • •

    RQ3 (Correlated Evidence and Role Balance): What distinct contributions come from long-range queues, correlation weighting, and role-balanced supervision?

  • •

    RQ4 (Longitudinal Evolution): Do gains persist across natural support strata (00, 11, 22–55, 66–1010, >10>10) and across distinct identities?

  • •

    RQ5 (Zero-Support Paradox): Through which inference pathways does individual evidence boost zero-support Answer-new targets?

  • •

    RQ6 (Robustness and Efficiency): How sensitive is INSPIRE to masking and evidence hyperparameters, and what overhead does Stage II incur?

3. Methodology

3.1. Overview and Two-Stage Decoupling

To unify zero-shot pattern transfer with sparse, correlated few-shot evidence, INSPIRE separates low-variance shared structural priors from posterior refinement for individual entities (Figure 2). Given catalog textual vectors xe∈ℝdxx_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} and predictor width dθd_{\theta}, training proceeds sequentially on the same chronological training split. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor (θ\theta) that maps query q=(h,r,?,t)q=(h,r,?,t) to a vector 𝐪θ∈ℝdθ\mathbf{q}_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}} conditioned on the relation and full-catalog log scores zθ​(q,o)≡zθ​(h,r,o,t)z_{\theta}(q,o)\equiv z_{\theta}(h,r,o,t), integrating Gated Memory Fusion (GMF), Full-Catalog Readout (FCR), Query-Side Masking (QSM), and Catalog-Side Masking (CSM). Subsequently, Stage II freezes the predictor θ\theta selected on validation, together with all external entity and relation tensors, and optimizes a lightweight Evidence Adaptation (EA) module (ϕ\phi) combining a Semantic Prior (SP), Long-Range Evidence (LRE), and Correlated Evidence Weighting (CEW) under support-stratified and Role-Balanced Supervision (RBS) with Co-Answer Set Supervision (CSS).

Rationale for decoupling. Since established entities generate over 95%95\% of natural stream traffic, end-to-end joint training invites dense gradients to drown out rare newcomers or causes high-capacity encoders to overfit sparse residuals. Therefore, freezing θ\theta anchors a stable global geometry while confining ϕ\phi to a regularized residual space. During evaluation, (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) remain fixed while revealed facts ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} advance persistent states strictly after timestamp tt is scored.

3.2. Stage I: Availability-Aware Predictor

Stage I builds on TransFIR’s interaction chain encoder, discrete behavioral codebook, pattern transfer, and candidate decoder (Zhao et al., 2026). For each query qj=(hj,rj,?,t)∈ℬtdq_{j}=(h_{j},r_{j},?,t)\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d}, the encoder maps hjh_{j}’s recent chain and rjr_{j} to 𝐪θ,j∈ℝdθ\mathbf{q}_{\theta,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}}, while pattern transfer produces a catalog table 𝐚e\mathbf{a}_{e} conditioned on the query and an initial pattern vector 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} for every e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}.

Event-updated entity memory. Following adaptive memory (Lee et al., 2026), each entity maintains a state 𝐦e,t∈ℝdθ\mathbf{m}_{e,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}} updated at each timestamp boundary via a learned retention gate ρ=σ⁡(ρraw)\rho=\sigma(\rho_{\mathrm{raw}}): 𝐦e←ρ​𝐦e+(1−ρ)​𝐪¯e,t\mathbf{m}_{e}\leftarrow\rho\mathbf{m}_{e}+(1-\rho)\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{e,t}, where 𝐪¯e,t\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{e,t} averages detached query vectors staged for head ee across both directions at tt (inactive entities retain 𝐦e\mathbf{m}_{e}). Committed states become readable only strictly after tt. However, restricting memory readout to 𝒰td\mathcal{U}_{t}^{d} leaves competing non-query candidates in stale representations and exacerbates Answer-new degradation. Let be∈{0,1}b_{e}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether entity ee has unmasked past memory or a current signal in 𝒰td\mathcal{U}_{t}^{d}. Coordinated availability masking (QSM and CSM). Since historical training batches are dominated by observed entities, unmasked training causes 𝐠e\mathbf{g}_{e} to rely excessively on memory and underperform on zero-support newcomers. 3.3. Stage II: Evidence Adaptation

Although Stage I builds a calibrated shared backbone, EMA memory compresses history into a single vector without separating long-range sparse facts from short-term bursts. Recalling our aforementioned Takata example (Figure 1(b)), retaining early isolated interactions (t=310,317t=310,317) alongside an independent partner (t=328t=328) while discounting repeated U.S. government demands (t=323,330t=323,330) requires explicit statistics at the event level. Hence, Stage II (EA) models each entity’s latent state in a compact space ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D} (D=64D=64) via correlated Bayesian updating.

Semantic Prior (SP) and Long-Range Evidence (LRE). To support zero-support entities (ke=0k_{e}=0) seamlessly, SP maps xex_{e} to an isotropic Gaussian prior mean 𝝁0,e∈ℝD\boldsymbol{\mu}_{0,e}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and precision λ0,e>0\lambda_{0,e}>0:

(8) 𝝁0,e=W0​xe,λ0,e=softplus⁡(𝐚0⊤​xe+b0)+ε,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{0,e}=W_{0}x_{e},\qquad\lambda_{0,e}=\operatorname{softplus}(\mathbf{a}_{0}^{\top}x_{e}+b_{0})+\varepsilon,

with ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6} and parameters (W0,𝐚0,b0)(W_{0},\mathbf{a}_{0},b_{0}) shared across ℰ\mathcal{E}. Furthermore, to avoid losing early sparse events to short temporal windows, LRE retrieves the latest ke≤Kk_{e}\leq K (K=32K=32) distinct original incident facts of ee from the entire revealed prefix ℋ<t\mathcal{H}_{<t} with unit age weights. For retained event ii, let 𝐫i∈ℝdθ\mathbf{r}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}} be the frozen directed relation vector, xni∈ℝdxx_{n_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} the counterpart’s text vector, and 𝐝i∈{(1,0),(0,1)}\mathbf{d}_{i}\in\{(1,0),(0,1)\} the direction indicator (incoming events use inverse relations with (0,1)(0,1); self-loops contribute one outgoing record). We decouple frozen normalized descriptors 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_{i} from learned surrogate observations 𝐲i∈ℝD\mathbf{y}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}:

(9) 𝐮i=[𝐫i;xni;𝐝i]‖[𝐫i;xni;𝐝i]‖2,𝐲i=WR​𝐫i+WN​xni+WD​𝐝i∈ℝD,\mathbf{u}_{i}=\frac{[\mathbf{r}_{i};x_{n_{i}};\mathbf{d}_{i}]}{\|[\mathbf{r}_{i};x_{n_{i}};\mathbf{d}_{i}]\|_{2}},\qquad\mathbf{y}_{i}=W_{R}\mathbf{r}_{i}+W_{N}x_{n_{i}}+W_{D}\mathbf{d}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D},

Correlated Evidence Weighting (CEW). Standard Bayesian Context Aggregation (Volpp et al., 2021) assumes independent observations, causing repeated bursts to inflate precision linearly. On the contrary, CEW models dependence between events via the descriptor Gram matrix He​He⊤H_{e}H_{e}^{\top} and computes generalized least-squares weights 𝐰e\mathbf{w}_{e}:

where 𝟏ke∈ℝke\mathbf{1}_{k_{e}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{e}} denotes the kek_{e}-dimensional vector of ones and γ=0.5\gamma=0.5. When ke=0k_{e}=0, δe=0\delta_{e}=0 and 𝜼e=𝟎\boldsymbol{\eta}_{e}=\mathbf{0} recover (𝝁0,e,λ0,e−1)(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{0,e},\lambda_{0,e}^{-1}) exactly. 3.4. Debiased Balanced Supervision

Since natural batches strongly favor high-support entities (Figure 1(c)), Stage II balances rare strata and roles via two equally weighted branches. However, naive balanced cross-entropy introduces an implicit Bayes prior-odds shift log⁡(πbal​(g)/πnat​(g))\log(\pi_{\mathrm{bal}}(g)/\pi_{\mathrm{nat}}(g)) across answer support strata g∈{0,…,4}g\in\{0,\dots,4\} (no(t)∈{0,1,2–5,6–10,>10}n_{o}(t)\in\{0,1,2\text{--}5,6\text{--}10,>10\}), which an unconstrained adapter can absorb as a blanket score bonus for zero-support candidates.

Training-only prior-odds debiasing. Let g⁡(e,t)∈{0,…,4}g(e,t)\in\{0,\dots,4\} denote candidate ee’s lifetime support stratum before tt. To counter the aforementioned prior-odds shift during training only, we add a learnable support bucket bias 𝐛train∈ℝ5\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{train}}\in\mathbb{R}^{5} anchored at mature entities (b~g=btrain,g−btrain,4\tilde{b}_{g}=b_{\mathrm{train},g}-b_{\mathrm{train},4}, b~4=0\tilde{b}_{4}=0), initialized to the closed-form training log-odds log⁡(πbal​(g)/πnat​(g))−log⁡(πbal​(4)/πnat​(4))\log(\pi_{\mathrm{bal}}(g)/\pi_{\mathrm{nat}}(g))-\log(\pi_{\mathrm{bal}}(4)/\pi_{\mathrm{nat}}(4)) without weight decay:

(15) sϕtr​(q,o)=sϕ​(q,o)+b~g⁡(o,t),pϕtr​(o∣q)=softmaxo⁡(sϕtr​(q,o)).s_{\phi}^{\mathrm{tr}}(q,o)=s_{\phi}(q,o)+\tilde{b}_{g(o,t)},\qquad p_{\phi}^{\mathrm{tr}}(o\mid q)=\operatorname{softmax}_{o}\big(s_{\phi}^{\mathrm{tr}}(q,o)\big).

Subsequently, at validation and test time, 𝐛train\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{train}} is discarded so that ranking relies exclusively on the unbiased scores sϕ​(q,o)s_{\phi}(q,o) (Equation 14).

Support-stratified and role-balanced branches. For any partition 𝒢\mathcal{G} with nonempty groups 𝒢+={G∈𝒢:|G|>0}\mathcal{G}^{+}=\{G\in\mathcal{G}:|G|>0\}, define

(16) Bal⁡(ℓ,𝒢)=1|𝒢+|​∑G∈𝒢+1|G|​∑j∈Gℓj\operatorname{Bal}(\ell,\mathcal{G})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}^{+}|}\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}^{+}}\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{j\in G}\ell_{j}

(zero if 𝒢+=∅\mathcal{G}^{+}=\emptyset). Rows in ℬtd\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d} are grouped by lifetime answer support noj​(t)n_{o_{j}}(t) (Equation 1) into five strata 𝒢sup\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sup}} (0,1,2​–​5,6​–​10,>100,1,2\text{--}5,6\text{--}10,>10) using cross-entropy ℓCE,j=−log⁡pϕtr​(oj∣qj)\ell_{\mathrm{CE},j}=-\log p_{\phi}^{\mathrm{tr}}(o_{j}\mid q_{j}), yielding ℒsup=Bal⁡(ℓCE,𝒢sup)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}=\operatorname{Bal}(\ell_{\mathrm{CE}},\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sup}}). To balance both endpoints, Role-Balanced Supervision (RBS) partitions eligible low-support rows into four role groups 𝒢role\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{role}}: Query-new, Answer-new, Both-new, and sparse rows observed at both endpoints having nhj​(t),noj​(t)>0n_{h_{j}}(t),n_{o_{j}}(t)>0 and minimum support min⁡(nhj​(t),noj​(t))≤5\min(n_{h_{j}}(t),n_{o_{j}}(t))\leq 5. Let 𝒜td​(h,r)\mathcal{A}_{t}^{d}(h,r) collect all distinct co-answers sharing (h,r)(h,r) in ℬtd\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d} (formed prior to grouping, keeping repeated rows as separate averaging units). Accordingly, Co-Answer Set Supervision (CSS) maximizes total mass on 𝒜td​(hj,rj)\mathcal{A}_{t}^{d}(h_{j},r_{j}):

(17) ℓCSS,j=−log∑o∈𝒜td​(hj,rj)pϕtr(o∣qj),ℒrole=Bal(ℓCSS,𝒢role).\ell_{\mathrm{CSS},j}=-\log\!\!\sum_{o\in\mathcal{A}_{t}^{d}(h_{j},r_{j})}\!\!p_{\phi}^{\mathrm{tr}}(o\mid q_{j}),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{role}}=\operatorname{Bal}(\ell_{\mathrm{CSS}},\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{role}}).

Soft residual alignment. Since Equation 15 is invariant to shifting rϕ​(q,o)r_{\phi}(q,o) up by cc on zero-support entities ℰ0​(t)={e:ne​(t)=0}\mathcal{E}_{0}(t)=\{e:n_{e}(t)=0\} and shifting b~0\tilde{b}_{0} down by cc, 𝐛train\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{train}} alone retains an additive gauge ambiguity. Writing r¯S​(q)=1|S|​∑o∈Srϕ​(q,o)\bar{r}_{S}(q)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{o\in S}r_{\phi}(q,o) over ℰ0​(t)\mathcal{E}_{0}(t) and ℰ>0​(t)=ℰ∖ℰ0​(t)\mathcal{E}_{>0}(t)=\mathcal{E}\setminus\mathcal{E}_{0}(t), we therefore anchor the residual gauge without altering ordering within each stratum:

(18) ℒalign=1|ℬtd|​∑q∈ℬtd(r¯ℰ0​(t)​(q)−r¯ℰ>0​(t)​(q))2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d}}\big(\bar{r}_{\mathcal{E}_{0}(t)}(q)-\bar{r}_{\mathcal{E}_{>0}(t)}(q)\big)^{2},

whenever both sets are nonempty, consequently yielding the Stage II objective

(19) ℒII=12​ℒsup+12​ℒrole+λalign​ℒalign.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{II}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{role}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}.

We average ℒsup\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}} and ℒrole\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{role}} equally (12\tfrac{1}{2} each) rather than introducing an extra trade-off hyperparameter specific to each dataset, thereby preserving the cross-entropy loss scale of a single supervision branch while weighting support-stratified and role-balanced gradients equally (removing RBS drops the second branch). In addition, the single global alignment weight λalign=0.2\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}=0.2 is selected strictly on validation splits (subsection 4.1).

3.5. Complexity Analysis

Algorithm 1 decouples offline training from state updates at timestamp boundaries. Since descriptors 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_{i} use frozen embeddings and fixed text, each entity’s Cholesky weights 𝐰e\mathbf{w}_{e}, precision δe\delta_{e}, and weighted raw relation, neighbor, and direction sums are cached and refreshed only when ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} modifies its queue; hence, by linearity, projecting cached sums via (WR,WN,WD)(W_{R},W_{N},W_{D}) recovers 𝜼e\boldsymbol{\eta}_{e} in Equation 10 without repeated Cholesky solves. For ata_{t} updated entities and descriptor width p=dθ+dx+2p=d_{\theta}+d_{x}+2, incremental refreshes cost O⁡(at​(K2​p+K3))O(a_{t}(K^{2}p+K^{3})), catalog projections cost O⁡(|ℰ|​p​D)O(|\mathcal{E}|pD), residual scoring costs O⁡(|ℬtd|​|ℰ|​D)O(|\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d}||\mathcal{E}|D), and queue storage is O⁡(|ℰ|​K)O(|\mathcal{E}|K). In parameter count, Stage II adds only 2​D​(dx+dθ)+dx+2​D+32D(d_{x}+d_{\theta})+d_{x}+2D+3 inference parameters (197,507197{,}507 at dx=dθ=768d_{x}=d_{\theta}=768; 230,275230{,}275 at dθ=1024d_{\theta}=1024), plus 55 training-only support bias scalars discarded before evaluation. Validation initializes with empty predictor memory and training prefix evidence queues, and testing carries validation states forward continuously.

4. Experiments

4.1. Experimental Setup

Datasets. We evaluate on four standard TKG benchmarks, namely ICEWS14, ICEWS18, ICEWS05–15, and GDELT, split chronologically into 50%/20%/30%50\%/20\%/30\% train/validation/test intervals following TransFIR (Zhao et al., 2026) and AdaTKG (Lee et al., 2026), which span distinct emergence regimes (Figure 1(c)). Specifically, ICEWS14 is short and moderately sparse (7,1287{,}128 entities, 304304 training snapshots, 246246 facts/snapshot), whereas ICEWS18 has the widest catalog (23,03323{,}033 entities) and highest debut concentration (70.35%70.35\% of cohort queries at support 00). In contrast, ICEWS05–15 spans the longest horizon (3,2433{,}243 training snapshots, 114114 facts/snapshot), where 83.32%83.32\% of cohort queries occur post-debut; finally, GDELT is highly dense (7,6917{,}691 entities, 2,1382{,}138 training snapshots, 811811 facts/snapshot) with severe skew (0.166%0.166\% emerging-query share).

Baselines. We compare against 18 baselines across four families: Graph-based (CyGNet (Zhu et al., 2021), RE-GCN (Li et al., 2021), HiSMatch (Li et al., 2022b), MGESL (Shi et al., 2024), LogCL (Chen et al., 2024), HisRES (Zhang et al., 2025b), MLEMKD (Qian et al., 2025)), Path-based (TLogic (Liu et al., 2022), TILP (Xiong et al., 2023), ECEformer (Fang et al., 2024), GenTKG (Liao et al., 2024)), Static Inductive (CompGCN (Vashishth et al., 2020), ICL (Lee et al., 2023a), PPT (Xu et al., 2023), MorsE (Chen et al., 2022), InGram (Lee et al., 2023b)), and Temporal Inductive (TransFIR (Zhao et al., 2026), AdaTKG (Lee et al., 2026)).

Evaluation protocol. Following subsection 2.1, all models perform raw, full-catalog bidirectional ranking over complete directional batches ℬtd\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d} strictly before ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} is revealed. Accordingly, consistent with subsection 2.2, we report Emerging MRR/H@3/H@10, endpoint role MRRs (Answer-new, Query-new, Both-new), and emerging-answer cohort MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}} and MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}}.

Results for the first three families follow (Zhao et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). TransFIR∗ and AdaTKG∗ are reproduced from their official implementations alongside INSPIRE w/o EA and INSPIRE under a fixed random seed. Checkpoints are selected by validation Emerging MRR (Stage II breaks ties by Answer-new, Both-new, and earlier epoch). Furthermore, to isolate Stage II cleanly, each dataset’s frozen Stage I predictor keeps the (pH,pC)(p_{H},p_{C}) selected on validation across Stage II ablations, while the single global alignment weight λalign=0.2\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}=0.2 is chosen strictly on the ICEWS14 and GDELT validation splits over {0,0.05,0.20,1.00}\{0,0.05,0.20,1.00\} prior to evaluation and fixed across all datasets.

Implementation settings. Table 1 lists the predictor widths and masking rates for each dataset alongside shared Stage II hyperparameters (D=64D=64, K=32K=32, γ=0.5\gamma=0.5, α>0\alpha>0, λalign=0.2\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}=0.2, unit age weights). Stage I optimizes with Adam (lr 10−410^{-4}, weight decay 10−510^{-5}, ≤1,000\leq 1{,}000 epochs), whereas Stage II uses AdamW (lr 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, ≤50\leq 50 epochs; training-only support bias 𝐛train\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{train}} uses lr 3×10−33\times 10^{-3} with zero weight decay and is discarded at evaluation). Both stages clip gradient norms at 1.01.0 with early stopping after 1111 epochs without improvement under fixed random seed 4242 on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. The official implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE.

4.2. Overall Performance (RQ1)

To answer RQ1, Table 2 compares INSPIRE against all 18 baselines on Emerging link prediction, and Table 3 further decomposes the four Temporal Inductive models by endpoint role and longitudinal cohort metrics.

Role asymmetry in baselines. Transductive graph, path, and static inductive baselines perform poorly on emerging entities since lookup embeddings and static structural transfer cannot track newly active actors as histories arrive. Furthermore, Table 3 exposes a severe endpoint role trade-off between the two strongest temporal inductive baselines: relative to TransFIR∗, AdaTKG∗ raises Query-new MRR across all four datasets by 12.3%12.3\%–37.4%37.4\%, yet consistently degrades Answer-new MRR by 5.7%5.7\%–14.6%14.6\% on the three ICEWS datasets and by 57.6%57.6\% on dense GDELT (0.0801→0.03400.0801\to 0.0340). This degradation is attributed to AdaTKG updating EMA memory primarily along query heads without calibrating catalog-wide candidate competition, allowing established candidates to drift ahead of unseen answer targets. Consequently, AdaTKG∗ also trails TransFIR∗ in cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} on three of the four datasets (dropping 51.8%51.8\% on GDELT).

Two-stage gains across roles and identities. On the contrary, INSPIRE resolves the aforementioned asymmetry progressively across its two stages. In Stage I, catalog-wide gated fusion (GMF, FCR) and availability masking allow INSPIRE w/o EA to surpass every baseline across all metrics in Table 2 and reverse AdaTKG’s Answer-new collapse on all four datasets, improving Answer-new MRR over AdaTKG∗ by 17.6%17.6\%–59.3%59.3\% on ICEWS and by 353.1%353.1\% on GDELT. Subsequently, Stage II EA builds directly on this calibrated backbone, adding a further 8.28%8.28\%–32.63%32.63\% relative Emerging MRR gain over INSPIRE w/o EA (+18.05%+18.05\% on ICEWS14, +24.33%+24.33\% on ICEWS18, +8.28%+8.28\% on ICEWS05–15, and +32.63%+32.63\% on GDELT) to outperform the strongest baseline by 16.73%16.73\%–88.83%88.83\% in MRR and up to 103.65%103.65\% in H@3. Moreover, these emerging gains do not sacrifice mature entities; instead, EA lifts overall test MRR over INSPIRE w/o EA on every dataset (0.4099→0.43050.4099\to 0.4305, 0.3082→0.31230.3082\to 0.3123, 0.5177→0.52530.5177\to 0.5253, and 0.1055→0.10840.1055\to 0.1084).

When decomposed by role (Table 3), Stage II delivers balanced improvements across both unseen endpoints rather than trading one role against the other. Specifically, relative to INSPIRE w/o EA, Query-new MRR rises by 9.29%9.29\%–21.94%21.94\% (achieving the top score on all three ICEWS datasets), Answer-new MRR rises by 7.81%7.81\%–41.24%41.24\% (reaching 0.21760.2176 on GDELT, a 2.7×2.7\times improvement over TransFIR∗ and 6.4×6.4\times over AdaTKG∗), and Both-new MRR increases by 40.21%40.21\% on ICEWS14 and 68.06%68.06\% on ICEWS18 (on ICEWS05–15, Both-new comprises only 8686 queries; on GDELT, only 22). In addition, cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} improves by 9.64%9.64\%–39.94%39.94\% over INSPIRE w/o EA (+16.93%+16.93\% to +150.54%+150.54\% over the strongest baseline), hence confirming that gains generalize beyond high-frequency newcomers.

4.3. Stage I Ablation (RQ2)

To evaluate RQ2, Table 4 ablates Stage I modules prior to EA against the complete Stage I predictor (INSPIRE w/o EA, denoted Full predictor):

  • •

    w/o CSM: disables catalog-side masking (pC=0p_{C}=0).

  • •

    w/o QSM+CSM: disables both training masks (pH=pC=0p_{H}=p_{C}=0).

  • •

    w/o FCR+CSM and w/o FCR+QSM+CSM: restrict memory readout to active query heads 𝒰td\mathcal{U}_{t}^{d} with QSM enabled and disabled, respectively.

  • •

    w/o GMF+QSM+CSM: zeroes 𝐠e=𝟎\mathbf{g}_{e}=\mathbf{0} with masks off, isolating the base pattern transfer backbone.

In addition, dedicated Stage II adapters are trained on every ablated predictor to examine cross-stage synergy (full paired tables appear in the supplementary material).

Memory fusion and catalog readout. Comparing w/o QSM+CSM against w/o GMF+QSM+CSM isolates GMF at zero masking: gated catalog fusion boosts pre-EA Emerging MRR across all four datasets by 9.3%9.3\%–110.0%110.0\% (+12.7%+12.7\% on ICEWS14, +40.7%+40.7\% on ICEWS18, +9.3%+9.3\% on ICEWS05–15, and +110.0%+110.0\% on GDELT), with even larger gains on Answer-new (+10.6%+10.6\%–+162.0%+162.0\%) and cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} (+10.7%+10.7\%–+141.0%+141.0\%). Furthermore, this advantage persists after pairing each variant with its own Stage II adapter (+9.1%+9.1\%–+26.6%+26.6\% paired Emerging MRR), hence demonstrating that Stage II cannot substitute for a Stage I representation calibrated across the catalog. Similarly, comparing w/o QSM+CSM with w/o FCR+QSM+CSM shows that enabling FCR at zero masking strengthens Answer-new and cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} on long-horizon ICEWS05–15 and dense GDELT (+15.3%+15.3\% Answer-new and +17.6%+17.6\% cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} on GDELT), where non-query catalog candidates accumulate dense histories that otherwise skew full-catalog competition.

Availability masking across stream regimes. Since QSM and CSM deliberately drop past entity memory during training to simulate zero-support inference, their standalone Stage I scores reflect an expected regularization trade-off that depends strongly on dataset length, catalog breadth, and density. To illustrate, on broad ICEWS18 dominated by zero-support debuts (23,03323{,}033 entities; 70.35%70.35\% zero-support debut share), masking prevents the fusion gate from overfitting mature actors. Although pre-EA w/o CSM shows slightly higher standalone Answer-new, pairing each predictor with Stage II reveals that full CSM delivers a substantial cross-stage advantage, surpassing paired w/o CSM by +13.2%+13.2\% Emerging, +23.6%+23.6\% Query-new, +31.0%+31.0\% Both-new, and +8.3%+8.3\% cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}}, attributed to EA refining a geometry already calibrated for absent history. Likewise, on short, sparse ICEWS14 (304304 snapshots), unmasked local readout (w/o FCR+QSM+CSM) fits the compact training graph slightly tighter prior to EA; nevertheless, once paired with Stage II, complete INSPIRE surpasses paired w/o FCR+QSM+CSM across Emerging, Query-new, Both-new (+10.6%+10.6\%), and cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}}, while CSM lifts paired Both-new by +7.2%+7.2\% and cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} by +2.4%+2.4\%. On the contrary, on long-horizon ICEWS05–15 (3,2433{,}243 snapshots, 83.32%83.32\% post-debut queries) and high-frequency GDELT (811811 facts/snapshot, 0.166%0.166\% emerging share), established temporal dynamics dominate; consequently, lighter or disabled masking (w/o QSM+CSM) preserves denser native patterns and achieves higher standalone and paired scores (0.26950.2695 and 0.20020.2002 paired Emerging MRR), consistent with validation selecting pC=0p_{C}=0 on GDELT. Therefore, availability masking acts as a regularizer sensitive to stream regimes that is most impactful on shorter streams or streams with higher debut ratios.

4.4. Stage II Ablation (RQ3)

For RQ3, Table 5 ablates Stage II EA components while holding the frozen Stage I predictor fixed per dataset under the debiased, aligned setting (α>0\alpha>0, 𝐛train\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{train}}, λalign=0.2\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}=0.2):

  • •

    w/o CEW: replaces CeC_{e} with independent covariance of matched marginal variance (1+γ)​I=1.5​I(1+\gamma)I=1.5I.

  • •

    w/o LRE: restricts queues to the last 1414 snapshots (retaining K=32K=32 and lifetime support labels).

  • •

    w/o CEW+LRE: removes both modules jointly (2×22\times 2 design).

  • •

    w/o RBS: removes the role-balanced branch (ℒII=ℒsup+λalign​ℒalign\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{II}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}).

Long-range evidence (LRE). Retaining sparse interactions over the full prefix lifts Emerging, Answer-new, Both-new, and cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} across all three ICEWS datasets. In particular, on sparse ICEWS18 with a broad catalog, LRE improves over w/o LRE by +4.3%+4.3\% Emerging, +10.2%+10.2\% Answer-new, +29.9%+29.9\% Both-new, and +14.1%+14.1\% cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}}, since emerging actors in geopolitical streams interact sporadically across long intervals and a 1414-snapshot window prematurely evicts informative early links. On the contrary, on highly dense GDELT (811811 facts/snapshot), rapid short-term news turnover causes older interactions to become less predictive of immediate links; hence, the 1414-snapshot window attains higher Emerging MRR (+7.5%+7.5\% over full prefix queues) at a slightly larger residual offset between zero-support and observed candidates, illustrating a temporal drift trade-off between sparse and high-frequency streams.

Correlated evidence weighting (CEW). Comparing INSPIRE against w/o CEW reveals a fundamental accuracy–calibration trade-off driven by bursty interaction redundancy (C2). Without correlation discounting, independent aggregation (1.5​I1.5I) excessively contracts posterior variance vo′v_{o^{\prime}} when established entities exhibit repetitive bursts, consequently inflating the variance contrast between zero-support and observed candidates. Although this uncalibrated contrast boosts Answer-new MRR in w/o CEW on bursty ICEWS18 and GDELT, it nevertheless degrades overall test MRR on all four datasets (0.43050.4305 vs. 0.42540.4254 on ICEWS14, 0.31230.3123 vs. 0.31050.3105 on ICEWS18, 0.52530.5253 vs. 0.52130.5213 on ICEWS05–15, and 0.10840.1084 vs. 0.10550.1055 on GDELT) while widening nontarget residual offsets. In contrast, with CEW, INSPIRE maintains the strongest full-catalog calibration on every dataset while improving Emerging and Query-new MRR on ICEWS14 and ICEWS05–15 and lifting Both-new MRR by +8.2%+8.2\% on ICEWS18.

Role-balanced supervision (RBS) and calibration verification. Removing RBS degrades Query-new MRR on every dataset (up to −9.2%-9.2\% on ICEWS18, where RBS lifts Emerging MRR by +7.4%+7.4\% and cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} by +9.3%+9.3\%) and reduces Emerging MRR on ICEWS05–15 (+2.8%+2.8\% gain from RBS) and GDELT (+5.5%+5.5\%), confirming that the role-balanced co-answer branch prevents support-stratified cross-entropy from neglecting unseen query heads. Furthermore, supplementary calibration controls verify that dropping gauge alignment (λalign=0\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}=0) leaks a blanket zero-support residual offset back into test scores (hurting overall test MRR), and that relative to a 11-parameter zero-support shortcut control (zθ(q,o)+β𝟏[no(t)=0]z_{\theta}(q,o)+\beta\mathbf{1}[n_{o}(t)=0]), calibrated INSPIRE lifts Query-new MRR by 18.1%18.1\%–40.0%40.0\% across all four datasets and doubles uncovered Answer-new MRR on ICEWS18 (0.01310.0131 vs. 0.00650.0065), confirming genuine semantic and structural discrimination.

4.5. Longitudinal Cohort Analysis (RQ4)

For RQ4, Figure 3 tracks the emerging-answer cohort 𝒞S\mathcal{C}_{S} across natural answer support strata (0,1,2​–​5,6​–​10,>100,1,2\text{--}5,6\text{--}10,>10).

Across ICEWS14 and ICEWS05–15, INSPIRE stays strictly above TransFIR∗, AdaTKG∗, and INSPIRE w/o EA in every support bin from zero-shot debut (00) to mature accumulation (>10>10) on both MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}} and MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}}. Specifically, on long-horizon ICEWS05–15 (83.32%83.32\% post-debut cohort queries), EA sustains positive gains even at >10>10 support (6,3296{,}329 queries, 198198 identities), outperforming TransFIR∗ by +14.1%+14.1\% in MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}} (0.34270.3427 vs. 0.30040.3004) and +13.3%+13.3\% in MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} (0.24040.2404 vs. 0.21210.2121). Similarly, on ICEWS14 at 22–55 support (330330 queries, 143143 identities), EA adds +10.5%+10.5\% MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}} and +10.0%+10.0\% MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} over INSPIRE w/o EA. Furthermore, on ICEWS18 and GDELT, INSPIRE leads all comparators throughout the entire zero-shot and few-shot range (00 through 66–1010): on ICEWS18 at 66–1010 support, EA lifts MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}} by +30.0%+30.0\% (0.1852→0.24070.1852\to 0.2407) and MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} by +40.8%+40.8\% (0.1263→0.17780.1263\to 0.1778), whereas on GDELT at support 11, EA more than doubles both MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}} (+128.6%+128.6\%) and MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} (+138.9%+138.9\%). Nevertheless, only in the small >10>10 tail of ICEWS18 (1616 identities) and GDELT (99 identities) does INSPIRE dip modestly below INSPIRE w/o EA, while remaining well above both temporal inductive baselines in MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}}.

4.6. Mechanism Analysis (RQ5)

Table 3raises a central question (RQ5): without prior shortcuts induced by balanced losses, how does EA boost Answer-new MRR by 7.81%7.81\%–41.24%41.24\% when target oo has zero prior events (ko=0k_{o}=0)? To answer this question, we freeze trained checkpoints (θ∗,ϕ∗)(\theta^{\ast},\phi^{\ast}), run seven inference switches (predictor only, prior residual only, full evidence, head events only, candidate events only, mean updates only, and variance updates only), and subsequently apply exact 2×22\times 2 Shapley allocations to partition the net event gain (Full−Prior\mathrm{Full}-\mathrm{Prior}) between head and candidate events (Figure 5).

Semantic prior and candidate score competition. Figure 5 shows that under α>0\alpha>0, both the learned Prior residual and Candidate events yield strictly positive Answer-new gains on every dataset, whereas Head events stay nearly zero or slightly negative. Specifically, on sparse ICEWS14 and long-horizon ICEWS05–15, textual priors contribute the largest share alongside positive candidate reinforcement; in contrast, on ICEWS18 with a broad catalog and dense GDELT, Candidate events drive 72.8%72.8\% and 69.9%69.9\% of the total gain. While unseen target oo remains at its prior (𝝁0,o,λ0,o−1)(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{0,o},\lambda_{0,o}^{-1}), correlated evidence updates competing established candidates o′≠oo^{\prime}\neq o, contracting vo′v_{o^{\prime}} and sharpening the Mahalanobis penalty dh,o′/Vh,o′d_{h,o^{\prime}}/V_{h,o^{\prime}} (Equation 14) to demote mismatched distractors. Furthermore, supplementary mean/variance decompositions across both roles confirm the coupled Gaussian effect: posterior variance contraction is strictly positive on Answer-new across all four datasets, whereas posterior mean updates act constructively on Query-new across ICEWS and on both roles in GDELT.

Selective promotion of moderately ranked targets. In addition, Figure 4 confirms the aforementioned mechanism across the Answer-new rank distribution: EA preserves 80%80\%–93%93\% of Rank-1 predictions, promotes 29%29\%–62%62\% of Rank 22–33 targets to Rank 1, lifts 30%30\%–57%57\% of Rank 44–1010 targets into Top-3, and moves 11%11\%–50%50\% of Rank 1111–100100 targets into Top-10. Meanwhile, 84%84\%–99%99\% of low-ranked (>100>100) targets remain >100>100 (0%0\% jumping to Rank 1 on ICEWS14, ICEWS05–15, and GDELT; <1%<1\% on ICEWS18), hence confirming selective competition refinement rather than blanket zero-support inflation.

4.7. Sensitivity and Efficiency (RQ6)

To answer RQ6, Figure 6 sweeps QSM (pH∈[0,0.5]p_{H}\in[0,0.5], step 0.10.1) and CSM (pC∈[0,0.5]p_{C}\in[0,0.5], step 0.050.05) along orthogonal 1D slices. Across all 6464 evaluated (pH,pC)(p_{H},p_{C}) pairs (1616 per dataset), debiased EA beats its paired Stage I predictor in Emerging, Answer-new, Cohort MRRmicro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{micro}}, and Cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} at every point (64/6464/64). Moreover, fixing Stage I predictors selected on validation leaves our reported GDELT Emerging MRR (0.16230.1623) conservative relative to neighboring sweep points (0.16500.1650–0.19710.1971).

Furthermore, Stage II hyperparameters are equally stable: on ICEWS14 and ICEWS18 (pH=pC=0.2p_{H}=p_{C}=0.2), validation Emerging MRR shifts by <0.0008<0.0008 between K=32K=32 and K=64K=64 (<0.0013<0.0013 across K∈{16,32,64}K\in\{16,32,64\}) and stays within 0.0040.004 across γ∈{0,0.1,0.5,1,2}\gamma\in\{0,0.1,0.5,1,2\} (positive γ\gamma consistently lifting Query-new over γ=0\gamma=0). In addition, Table 6 shows that freezing θ\theta and caching Cholesky sums (subsection 3.5) keeps Stage II peak GPU memory to 2.172.17–8.248.24 GiB and training time to 23%23\%–41%41\% of Stage I on ICEWS (62%62\% on GDELT); extended latencies appear in the supplement.

Paradigm synthesis. Therefore, RQ1–RQ6 distill two general principles: (i) capacity–sparsity decoupling freezes a shared backbone calibrated for history availability while fitting a compact correlation-weighted residual to avoid sparse overfitting, and (ii) catalog-wide competition matters as much as newcomer encoding, since accurately calibrating established distractors enables emerging actors to surface reliably from debut through sparse growth.

5. Related Work

Temporal history and event forecasting. Early dynamic encoders modeled continuous TKG evolution via temporal point processes (Know-Evolve (Trivedi et al., 2017)), recurrent neighborhood aggregation (RE-Net (Jin et al., 2020)), and neural differential equations (TANGO (Han et al., 2021b)). Subsequently, snapshot models refined historical reuse through copy–generation modes (CyGNet (Zhu et al., 2021)), relation-aware graph convolutions (RE-GCN (Li et al., 2021)), and local–global repetition (TiRGN (Li et al., 2022a)). Furthermore, recent works model query–candidate subgraphs (HiSMatch (Li et al., 2022b)), multigranularity hypergraphs (MGESL (Shi et al., 2024)), local–global contrastive learning (LogCL (Chen et al., 2024)), concurrent and evolutionary multigraphs (LMS (Zhang et al., 2024)), and query relevance structuring (HisRES (Zhang et al., 2025b)). However, since these transductive models depend on entity lookup tables and dense histories, accuracy degrades sharply for emerging entities.

Structural, logical, and language model reasoning. Symbolic and structural approaches extract interpretable evidence via temporal subgraphs and logical rules (xERTE (Han et al., 2021a), TLogic (Liu et al., 2022), TILP (Xiong et al., 2023)), evolutionary event chain Transformers (ECEformer (Fang et al., 2024)), and hybrid inductive–deductive–abductive hypergraph reasoning (Tian et al., 2026). In addition, language model approaches serialize facts into time-aware or in-context prompts (PPT (Xu et al., 2023), ICL (Lee et al., 2023a)), generative decoding guided by retrieved rules (GenTKG (Liao et al., 2024)), and topology-guided LLM logical learning (Gao et al., 2026). On the contrary, INSPIRE performs full-catalog discriminative ranking that unites textual priors with correlation-adjusted statistics over long-range prefixes.

Inductive transfer and adaptive entities. Static inductive methods generalize beyond fixed vocabularies via relational compositions or meta-knowledge (CompGCN (Vashishth et al., 2020), MorsE (Chen et al., 2022), InGram (Lee et al., 2023b), ULTRA (Galkin et al., 2024)), whereas distributed and federated graph systems study collaborative alignment over decentralized dynamic graphs (Islam et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025c; Zheng and Cai, 2020; Zheng et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025). In temporal settings, OntoTKGE (Lin et al., 2026) transfers concept dynamics via ontologies, TransFIR (Zhao et al., 2026) maps unseen entities to behavioral codebooks via textual clusters, and AdaTKG (Lee et al., 2026) maintains online per-entity EMA memory. Nevertheless, TransFIR omits catalog-wide dynamic memory and AdaTKG’s updates centered on active queries degrade Answer-new ranking (Table 3); hence, INSPIRE resolves this gap in Stage I via GMF, FCR, QSM, and CSM.

Few-shot adaptation and correlated evidence. Few-shot TKG models target scarce observations through meta-learned neighbor aggregation (MetaTKGR (Wang et al., 2022)) or mutual distillation (MLEMKD (Qian et al., 2025)). Furthermore, freezing pretrained backbones while tuning compact adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019) or retrieval caches (Zhang et al., 2022) supports data-efficient specialization, whereas Set Transformer (Lee et al., 2019) and Bayesian Context Aggregation (Volpp et al., 2021) aggregate variable-size sets via attention or independent Gaussian updates. Accordingly, Stage II (EA) adapts this Bayesian updating paradigm over a frozen backbone to full-catalog TKG ranking with closed-form CEW over bounded LRE queues under debiased RBS and CSS.

6. Conclusion

Forecasting links for emerging entities in TKGs requires reasoning across a skewed continuum from zero-support debuts to sparse, bursty trajectories. To address the aforementioned challenge, we presented INSPIRE, a two-stage framework decoupling availability-aware shared patterns (GMF, FCR, QSM, CSM) from lightweight evidence adaptation (EA) with textual priors, long-range queues, Gram matrix correlation weighting, and debiased, aligned balanced supervision.

Across all four benchmarks, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%16.73\%–88.83%88.83\% over the strongest baselines, resolves adaptive memory Answer-new degradation, lifts overall test MRR on every dataset, and sustains cohort MRRmacro\operatorname{MRR}_{\mathrm{macro}} gains across support growth. Furthermore, decompositions and rank transition analyses at fixed checkpoints attribute calibrated Answer-new gains to semantic priors and candidate score competition, demoting mismatched established distractors and promoting plausible moderately ranked newcomers without zero-support shortcuts.

Finally, beyond preregistered catalogs and static names, promising future directions include open-vocabulary entity discovery under alias drift, evolving multimodal priors or priors grounded in documents, and selective forgetting adaptive to regime shifts with asynchronous inference on individual queries.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
